newsitem.title: USA: Clinton woos Texas voters at Alamo rally.
newsitem.headline: Clinton woos Texas voters at Alamo rally.

text.p: President Bill Clinton plunged into the final weekend of his campaign for re-election on Saturday by visiting the Alamo, where he compared himself to Texas heroes for standing up to Congress on the budget.

Addressing a large, friendly crowd at a rally at the shrine of Texas liberty, Clinton recalled his policy scrap with the Republicans late last year that twice shut the government, and said, "I thought about the Alamo."
"They said, 'Oh, the president will cave. He won't be able to stand letting the government close.' We had this economy rocking along ... and they were threatening to default on our debt," he said.

"They said, "Oh, he'll blink.' And I said, 'You know, I'd a lot rather see the American people hurt for two or three weeks or two or three months than 20 or 30 years. Shut her down, I'm not going to buy your budget'," Clinton said.

Clinton, striving to become the first Democrat since Jimmy Carter in 1976 to win normally pro-Republican Texas with its 32 electoral votes, was carrying on a presidential campaign tradition in visiting the Alamo.

The tradition reportedly began a century ago with President Benjamin Harrison, who is said to have spoken at the chapel where Jim Bowie, Davy Crockett and 187 others died after refusing to retreat in a war for Texas independence from Mexico in 1836.
"Today is the beginning of a new day for presidential politics in Texas. We're going to carry Texas for Bill Clinton on Tuesday!" former Texas Gov. Ann Richards said in an impassioned warmup speech.
Clinton, accompanied by his wife Hillary, said that if a Republican president had compiled an economic record as good as his is, "They'd be saying that the president can virtually levitate."

"What do you think the Republicans would be saying if they had a president who had presided over an administration that had cut the deficit by 63 percent, that had the highest job growth rate of any Republican administration in 70 years, that had the lowest average unemployment in 20 years, the lowest average inflation in 30 years?" he asked.
"They'd be saying, 'It is morning in America'," Clinton said.

Foregoing the kind of around-the-clock campaigning that Republican Bob Dole is doing before Tuesday's election, Clinton planned an airport rally in his hometown of Little Rock, Arkansas, later on Saturday before ending the day trying to nail down victory in Florida.

U.S. presidential elections are actually 51 separate contests in each of the 50 states and the District of Columbia to choose stand-ins for the candidates called electors. A total of 270 electoral votes are needed for victory.

In his weekly radio address, which he taped in Las Cruces, New Mexico, on Friday night, Clinton deplored "old politics of division" in an indirect but obvious salvo at Dole and the Republicans, who have hammered away at his ethics and character in the closing days of the campaign.
Without mentioning his opponents by name, Clinton said that instead of bringing people together, "The old politics of division tried to drive wedges between us, to take advantage of our fears."

"Many people use elections to divide us. But I believe this election can unite us to go forward together. When we come together to find common ground, we are stronger as a nation and there is no challenge we can't meet," he said.

Clinton has been accused of practicing divisive politics by the Republicans, who say he has tried to scare people into believing they would gut Medicare and Medicaid health benefits for the elderly, poor and disabled and many other popular domestic programs.
